keyConcepts: Lexical scope — visibility determined by where function is written, not where called
Closure — inner function keeps outer variables alive even after outer scope is gone
Closures capture the variable, not the value
var is function-scoped — one variable shared across all loop iterations
let is block-scoped — fresh variable per iteration
addEventListener registers a function for later — does NOT run it immediately
Call stack — LIFO, runs synchronous code
Microtask queue — Promise callbacks, await continuations — drained fully before any macrotask
Macrotask queue — setTimeout, I/O — one per event loop tick
Event loop — stack empty → drain microtasks → one macrotask → repeat
libuv — C library under Node.js with thread pool for actual I/O
await — pauses the function, frees the JS thread
async — marks function as suspendable (state machine)
Promise — object representing a future value (pending/fulfilled/rejected)
Blocking — while loop holds stack, event loop stuck
Non-blocking — yields stack immediately, event loop free
syllabusTopics: TypeScript type system (generics, conditional types, mapped types)
TypeScript utility types (Partial, Required, Pick, Omit, Record, Exclude)
Web APIs (setTimeout, fetch, Web Workers, Microtasks)
Design patterns in JS (Module, Observer, Singleton, Factory)
Functional programming (pure functions, immutability, higher-order functions)
Performance patterns (debounce, throttle, memoization, lazy loading)

qa.question: Your Node.js API handler has a `while(Date.now() < start + 5000)` loop before res.send(). The service handles 500 req/sec. What happens to those requests and why?
qa.answer: All incoming requests are blocked for 5 seconds. The while loop holds the call stack — the event loop can't pick up anything. Node.js is single-threaded, so no other request handler runs until the loop finishes. Fix: use async I/O (await setTimeout or actual async DB calls) to yield the stack so the event loop can process other requests.

qa.question: What's the output order? `console.log('A'); setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C')); console.log('D');`
qa.answer: A → D → C → B. A and D run synchronously. C is a microtask (Promise) — microtasks drain before any macrotask. B is a macrotask (setTimeout) — runs last.

qa.question: You write `async function handler() { const user = await db.getUser(id); res.send(user); }`. Does this create a new thread? Who actually fetches from the DB?
qa.answer: No new thread. libuv (C library under Node.js) has a thread pool that does actual I/O. The JS thread hands the operation to libuv and is immediately free. When DB responds, libuv puts the callback in the event queue. The event loop picks it up, Promise resolves, await resumes the function, and res.send runs.

qa.question: 500 concurrent requests all hit `await db.getUser()` at the same time. Walk me through what the Node.js thread is doing.
qa.answer: Thread hits await on req1, drops it (stack free), picks up req2, hits await, drops it, ... all 500 reach await within milliseconds. Thread goes idle. As DB responses arrive, libuv puts callbacks in the event queue. Thread drains the queue: res.send for req1, req2, etc. Thread was never stuck — it was never sitting idle waiting for any single request.

qa.question: This loop attaches click handlers: `for (var i = 0; i < 5; i++) { btn[i].addEventListener('click', () => console.log(i)); }`. Every button logs 5. Why, and two fixes?
qa.answer: var is function-scoped — one shared i across all iterations. addEventListener registers the function for later, not immediately. By click time, loop has finished and i=5. All 5 closures reference the same i. Fix 1: use let (block-scoped, fresh i per iteration). Fix 2: IIFE — wrap in (function(j){...})(i) to capture i by value in a new scope.

qa.question: A teammate writes `var processOrder = function(){...}` inside an `if` block and calls it outside. It works when the condition is true but crashes with TypeError when false. What's happening and how do you fix it?
qa.answer: var is function-scoped — it hoists to the top of the containing function as undefined, ignoring the if block. When condition is false, processOrder is never assigned, so calling undefined() throws TypeError. Fix: use const + ternary to handle both branches, or move the call inside the if block with const declaration.

qa.question: What's the difference between accessing a `var` before its declaration vs accessing a `let` before its declaration?
qa.answer: var: returns undefined — it's hoisted and initialized to undefined. let: throws ReferenceError — it's hoisted but sits in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until the declaration line. TDZ starts at block entry, ends at the let/const declaration.

qa.question: Why does calling a function declaration before it's defined work, but calling a function expression (var fn = function(){}) before it's defined throws TypeError — not ReferenceError?
qa.answer: Function declarations are fully hoisted — both the variable and the function body. Function expressions with var: only the variable is hoisted (as undefined), not the assignment. So calling it before the assignment means calling undefined(), which is TypeError (not a function), not ReferenceError (variable doesn't exist).

qa.question: You have 10,000 User objects. A teammate defines getFullName() inside the constructor. What's the problem and how do you fix it?
qa.answer: Every new User() creates a brand new copy of getFullName — 10,000 copies of identical function in memory. Fix: move it to User.prototype.getFullName. One shared copy, all instances find it via prototype chain. Rule: own data (unique per instance) → this in constructor. Methods (same logic for all) → on prototype.

qa.question: What's the difference between Person.greet = fn and Person.prototype.greet = fn?
qa.answer: Person.greet = fn is a static method — sits on the function object itself, called as Person.greet(). Person.prototype.greet = fn is an instance method — inherited by all instances via prototype chain, called as p1.greet(). Java equivalent: static method vs instance method.

qa.question: A teammate says 'JS class inheritance is completely different from prototype-based inheritance.' Are they right?
qa.answer: No. class is syntactic sugar over prototype chains. Methods defined in a class body are placed on ClassName.prototype automatically. The underlying mechanism — [[Prototype]] links, chain lookup, new doing 4 steps — is identical. class just makes it look like Java.

qa.question: You're publishing a Node.js utility library. How do you make it work for both CJS (require) and ESM (import) consumers?
qa.answer: Use the exports field in package.json with import and require conditions pointing to separate build outputs (e.g. dist/index.mjs for ESM, dist/index.cjs for CJS). Build tools like tsup or rollup generate both from one source. Node.js picks the right one automatically based on how the consumer imports it.

qa.question: Why does ESM support tree shaking but CommonJS doesn't?
qa.answer: ESM imports are static — resolved at parse time before code runs. Bundlers can analyze exactly what's used at build time and eliminate the rest. CJS require() is dynamic — the path can be computed at runtime (e.g. require(condition ? 'a' : 'b')). Bundlers can't know what's unused, so nothing gets eliminated.

qa.question: You need to fetch getUserProfile(), getUserSettings(), getUserNotifications() — all independent. Teammate uses three sequential awaits. What's wrong and what's the fix?
qa.answer: Sequential awaits run one at a time — 300ms * 3 = 900ms total. Since calls are independent, use Promise.all: const [profile, settings, notif] = await Promise.all([...]). All three run in parallel — 300ms total. Use sequential only when call B depends on call A's result.

qa.question: When do you use Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled?
qa.answer: Promise.all: all calls must succeed to proceed — fails fast if any rejects, returns values directly. Use for page data where partial load is useless. Promise.allSettled: partial success is acceptable — waits for all, returns {status, value/reason} per item. Use for independent dashboard widgets where you want to show whatever succeeded.

qa.question: Your Timer class has setInterval with a regular function inside start(). this.seconds logs NaN. Why and how do you fix it?
qa.answer: setInterval calls the callback as a plain function — no object before the dot, no new. Default binding applies: this = window (or undefined in strict mode). this.seconds++ on window = NaN. Fix 1 (modern): use arrow function — it inherits this from start() which is the Timer instance. Fix 2 (legacy): capture const self = this before setInterval and use self inside.

qa.question: What's the difference between call, apply, and bind? When would you use each?
qa.answer: call: invokes immediately, args comma-separated. apply: invokes immediately, args as array (use when args are already in an array, e.g. Math.max.apply(null, arr)). bind: returns a NEW function with this permanently fixed, call it later. Use bind when passing a method as a callback and need to preserve this.
